title: Iran’s efforts to offset US naval blockade fall short, economists warn
html:
Iranian economists have warned that alternative trade routes and domestic economic measures cannot fully offset the loss of oil revenues caused by the US naval blockade, despite assurances from Tehran that the country can withstand the pressure.

The warnings come as Washington points to the growing impact of the blockade on Iran’s oil exports.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that Iran had exhausted its floating oil stocks and had not loaded a tanker since Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently said the economic damage inflicted by the blockade had been so significant that President Donald Trump no longer saw a need for a large-scale military operation.

Oil exports suffer as Iran seeks alternative routes

Before Washington first imposed its naval blockade in April, Iran exported approximately 1.5 million barrels of crude oil a day to China, its largest customer. The United States reinstated the blockade in July.

In recent months, Iran has reportedly exported limited quantities of petroleum products, including fuel oil and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), by road to neighboring countries such as Pakistan and Afghanistan. Some natural gas and jet fuel have also reportedly been transferred through ship-to-ship operations east of the Strait of Hormuz.

Writing in the economic daily Donya-ye Eqtesad on October 18, economic analyst Hamid Mollazadeh argued that these limited exports could not compensate for the loss of crude oil shipments.

Iranian officials and some Iranian media outlets have promoted land routes as an alternative for exporting oil and importing goods, but economists have warned of their limited capacity.

Energy expert Hamid Hosseini wrote in the reformist newspaper Shargh on November 2 that potential exports to Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan, Turkey, and Iraq’s Kurdistan Region could collectively reach no more than 250,000 to 300,000 barrels a day.

That would amount to no more than a fifth of Iran’s previous crude exports to China.

Hosseini argued that overcoming the blockade would require a diplomatic solution.

Pouya Jabal Ameli, editor-in-chief of Donya-ye Eqtesad, warned in a September 21 editorial that even with alternative export routes, Iran’s foreign currency revenues could fall to approximately one-fifth of their pre-blockade levels.

He said oil revenues had previously accounted for around 35% of government funding, making it difficult to cover the shortfall in the near term without resorting to inflationary policies.

Jabal Ameli estimated that even under the most optimistic assessments, 40% of Iran’s population was already living below the poverty line before the blockade because of sanctions.

He warned that the latest restrictions could push at least two more income deciles into poverty by the end of the Iranian calendar year in March 2027.

In a separate October 5 article published by Eghtesad Ba Ma, he argued that monetary and foreign exchange policies alone could not resolve the crisis and that improving Iran’s international relations was necessary to give businesses a clearer economic outlook.

Economists warn of mounting pressure on government finances

The economic consequences extend beyond lost oil revenues.

Economist Morteza Afghah told Shargh last week that the prolonged military standoff and continuing blockade would put further pressure on Iran’s economy and government finances.

He said the mere prospect of war created uncertainty and discouraged investment, while actual trade restrictions and the naval blockade compounded the damage.

Afghah said short-term measures such as selling state-owned companies, borrowing from the Central Bank and issuing government bonds, all used under former President Hassan Rouhani, could not replace oil revenues in the long run.

Others argue that Iran can cushion some of the economic damage.

Saeed Leilaz, an economist affiliated with the centrist Executives of Construction Party who opposes concessions to Washington, told state television’s Jahan Ara program on Tuesday that the blockade represented the greatest economic shock in Iran’s history.

He said the blockade should be treated like a military conflict but argued that Iran could withstand its effects through sound economic policies and efforts to combat corruption.

Disruptions to imports raise concerns

Beyond disrupting maritime trade, the blockade has also restricted Iran’s access to the foreign currency needed to finance imports.

At least 75% of Iran's foreign trade was previously conducted by sea. The blockade has effectively eliminated the possibility of importing nonessential goods by sea.

Officials have sought to ease concerns over supplies, pointing to strategic reserves and alternative routes for imports.

On Wednesday, First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref sought to reassure the public, saying increased cargo unloading and customs clearance at border crossings outside southern Iran showed the country could withstand the US naval blockade.

He said stocks of essential and strategic goods were in good condition and called for measures to prevent prices of basic goods from rising for at least three months.

Consumer prices in October were 88.7% higher than a year earlier, while food and beverage prices rose 112.6% year-on-year, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.

To illustrate the capacity of Iran’s land borders, Leilaz cited official estimates putting annual smuggling at $35 billion. He argued that the figure could reach $50 billion without intervention by law enforcement authorities.

Although he acknowledged that shortages and difficulties were inevitable in some sectors, he maintained that a country with thousands of kilometers of land borders could not face a severe import crisis.

Washington has also announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at restricting the movement of weapons and sanctioned materials across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that Iran’s size and extensive cross-border trade made a land blockade nearly impossible to enforce.

Hardliners call for military action to break blockade

Hardliners, meanwhile, have called for military action to break the blockade rather than relying on alternative trade routes or negotiations.

The hardline newspaper Kayhan has described negotiations with Washington as an “operation of deception,” arguing that military action is needed to break the blockade.

The newspaper has called for Iranian attacks on oil facilities and US companies in the region in response to the blockade, arguing that such action could increase pressure on Washington from regional countries.

Hardliners have also called in recent days for Iranian oil tankers to challenge the blockade, although no practical action has been taken so far.

In an October 21 article, Jam-e Jam, a newspaper affiliated with state broadcaster IRIB, argued that breaking the blockade could both restore oil revenues and end the prolonged military standoff.

The competing approaches highlight the divisions within Iran over how to respond to Washington's pressure: whether to rely on economic adaptation and diplomacy, or to pursue a more confrontational strategy aimed at forcing the United States to reconsider the blockade.

Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported on Wednesday, citing informed sources, that Kataib Hezbollah had transferred large quantities of military equipment to western Iraq and established new military positions.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the Critical Threats Project (CTP) said in a separate report that Iran-backed Iraqi militias had threatened and reportedly drawn up plans in recent weeks to attack US assets if the United States and Israel resumed strikes on Iran.

Esmail Qaani, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force, traveled to Baghdad last week and held talks with senior Iraqi militia leaders in an effort to defuse tensions between Kataib Hezbollah and the Iraqi government.

A senior member of Iraq’s Iran-backed Badr Organization previously told Iraqi Kurdish media that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Qaani had reached a written draft agreement to redeploy some Kataib Hezbollah forces to western Anbar province, ISW-CTP said.

The institutes also assessed that Iran-backed Iraqi militias were almost certainly behind drone surveillance of the US Embassy in Baghdad in October, describing it as an attempt to deter Washington from striking Iran.

Militia retains control of Jurf al-Sakhar

Iraqi government security forces had not entered the core areas controlled by Kataib Hezbollah in Jurf al-Sakhar, five days after Iraqi forces began deploying to the area, Al-Mada reported.

The militia had received fresh reinforcements, while Iranian and Houthi advisers remained in the area, according to the report.

The newspaper said the Iraqi army’s deployment had been limited and that federal police had merely reorganized their existing presence without taking control of additional territory.

Zaidi last week ordered Kataib Hezbollah to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakhar, which the militia has controlled since 2014, after Iraqi officials accused the group of operating an oil-smuggling network that diverted hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state-owned oil.

Kataib Hezbollah denied the allegations, describing them as part of a campaign to force it to surrender its weapons.

Iraqi security forces began deploying to the area on Friday under a negotiated compromise aimed at averting an armed confrontation. Under the agreement, Kataib Hezbollah fighters were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq.

Militia fighters integrated into state forces

More than 2,000 Kataib Hezbollah members have been incorporated into the militia-affiliated 72nd and 79th brigades of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), according to Al-Mada.

Previously paid directly by the militia, the fighters will now receive state-funded salaries and benefit from official institutional protection, the sources told Al-Mada.

ISW-CTP said integrating the fighters into the PMF did not reduce the threat they posed to US interests, arguing that brigades controlled by Iran-backed Iraqi militias answer to Tehran rather than the Iraqi prime minister.

The institutes assessed that the integration may be part of Zaidi’s efforts to balance US demands for the disarmament of militias with Kataib Hezbollah’s insistence on retaining its weapons.

Designated a terrorist organization by the United States, Kataib Hezbollah is among Iran’s most powerful militia allies in Iraq and has resisted calls to disarm amid mounting US pressure on Baghdad to bring armed factions under state control.

The group is among several Iraqi militias that have claimed attacks on US forces in Persian Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The combative rhetoric came as US officials claimed their blockade and sanctions campaign had brought Iranian oil exports to a standstill, depriving Tehran of a vital source of revenue.

Hassan Hassanzadeh, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in Greater Tehran, said Iran's defense, missile and drone capabilities were “increasing day by day.”

“If the United States and Israel make another mistake, they will witness the unveiling of new targets, weapons and offensive plans,” he said.

Iran also directed its warnings at Arab countries in the Persian Gulf, accusing several of knowingly facilitating US and Israeli attacks by providing access to their territory, airspace, military facilities and logistical resources.

Iran's representative to the United Nations said those countries were legally obliged to compensate Tehran fully for the resulting damage.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that Iran had exhausted its floating oil stocks and failed to load a single tanker since Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August.

“The Iranian regime is a sinking ship,” Bessent wrote on X, adding that Iran “doesn’t have a drop of oil on the water left to sell.”

The economic pressure has also been reflected in Iran's currency, which fell to another record low on Tuesday, with the dollar reaching 2.856 million rials on Tehran's open market after Washington imposed fresh sanctions on Iranian financial networks.

But Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said statements by American military commanders showed Washington was struggling to sustain the blockade.

He predicted that military exhaustion and mounting financial costs would force the United States to abandon its blockade and withdraw its forces from the region.

Mohebbi, however, said Washington would soon discover that its blockade was futile. He said Iran's armed forces remained fully prepared in equipment, resources and morale.

Meanwhile, China urged Washington and Tehran to keep the door to negotiations open, with Beijing's ambassador to Iran, Cong Peiwu, saying Wednesday that de-escalation and a return to talks should be the immediate priorities.

Cong said China supported a diplomatic settlement of the nuclear dispute and efforts to reach a comprehensive agreement over the Strait of Hormuz.

Amirhossein Bankipour, a member of parliament's Cultural Committee, said young Iranians faced a growing gap between sexual maturity and the means to start a household. Only 1 percent of young men and 20 percent of young women under 20 marry, he said.

"Our first solution is marriage, and if that is not possible, the second is chastity and modesty. But if these solutions alone are insufficient, we should not ignore the problem and must consider other options," he said.

His third option is a long engagement in law. In Iran, couples often sign a marriage contract, known as aqd, months before they hold a wedding and move in together. Bankipour proposed stretching that period to four or five years, until the couple has a job, a home or enough money to live on.

Official figures show how far marriage has slipped out of reach. Iran registered 431,415 marriages in the year to March 2026, down 8.8 percent from the year before and about half the 891,627 recorded in 2010, according to the national population headquarters, which cited civil registration data.

The average age at first marriage has risen to 28.2 for men and 24.1 for women.

Officials blame rising housing costs, dowry expenses, inflation and job insecurity. With inflation near 89 percent and rents a third higher than a year ago, some couples who divorce now cannot afford to move out of the home they shared.

Under Iranian law, sex outside marriage is a crime, which leaves young Iranians few legal options for intimacy.

One of them is temporary marriage, known in Persian as sigheh, a practice recognized in Shiite jurisprudence. Unlike permanent marriage, a sigheh has an agreed duration and a set dowry. It can last from a few hours to several years and ends without divorce.

Religious authorities present it as a way to meet sexual needs without breaking Islamic law. Bankipour did not explicitly propose it, but his remarks revive a long debate over how far marriage contracts can be stretched to fit lives that marriage no longer fits.

Sigheh's legal standing has not brought social acceptance. Even in religious families, it carries a stigma, especially for women, Iran International has reported.

Temporary marriage has also given commercial sex a legal cover.

A May 2025 Iran International investigation found online platforms offering paid encounters marketed as Islamic marriage. Intermediaries advertised women by age, appearance, education and location, offering arrangements from a few hours to monthly contracts. Contacts with several operators showed that some arranged real meetings rather than simply defrauding customers.

Iran's cyber police later acknowledged the spread of such platforms but described many as scams. Prostitution is banned in Iran.
